title: Creating Adhesive and Soluble Gradients for Imaging Cell Migration with Fluorescence Microscopy
protocol: Submerge glass coverslips in 100% ethanol and place them in a sonicating bath for 30 min.
Dry the glass coverslips in air or under a stream of nitrogen.
Sonicate the glass coverslips for 30 min in 1 M NaOH.
Rinse the glass surfaces by dipping them carefully in a beaker filled with 1.5 L Milli-Q H2O.
Repeat the rinsing process three times using fresh Milli-Q H2O each time.
Dry the glass coverslips in an oven at 60 °C.
Place half of the clean glass coverslips individually in a humid chamber made of a 24-well plate partially filled with H2O.
Drop 15 μl of PLL-PEG-biotin (1 mg/ml) in PBS on each glass coverslip.
Sandwich the PEG solution carefully between the remaining half of the clean glass coverslips.
Incubate the coverslips for 1 hour in the humid chamber.
Gently slide the sandwiched coverslips apart without scraping the PEG-coated surface.
Rinse the coverslips with Milli-Q H2O.
Air-dry the glass coverslips on paper towel with the treated surface facing upward if necessary.
Store the glass coverslips in a vacuum desiccator until further use.
Clean the silicon wafer by incubating it in piranha solution (3:1 v:v of sulphuric acid and 30% hydrogen peroxide) for 20 min.
Rinse the wafer thoroughly with MilliQ H2O ten times.
Dry the wafer in an oven at 150 °C overnight.
Rinse the clean and dried silicon wafer with 100% acetone.
Rinse the silicon wafer with 100% isopropyl alcohol.
Spin-coat 2 ml of GM1070 SU-8 photoresist onto the wafer at 3,100 rpm for 40 sec to create a 25 μm thick layer.
Bake the sample on a hot plate at 65 °C for 5 min.
Further bake the sample at 95 °C for 5 min.
Expose the SU-8 photoresist to UV light for 60 sec under a photomask with the desired pattern.
Repeat the baking process described in the protocol.
Develop the sample by immersing the wafer in SU-8 developer for 4 min.
Rinse the sample in 100% isopropyl alcohol.
Dry the sample under nitrogen flow.
Mix 1 part (w/w) of curing agent with 10 parts of elastomer prepolymer (Sylgard 184).
Degas the mixture in a desiccator attached to a vacuum line for 1 hr.
Pour the PDMS elastomer onto the silicon master inside a Petri dish to about 1 cm in height.
Cure the master and PDMS mixture in an oven at 70 °C for 1 hr.
Remove the PDMS stamp from the silicon master.
Cut the PDMS stamp to size.
Passivate glass coverslips.
Print protein patterns with microcontact printing.
Use dip-pen lithography to transfer a small volume of solution onto the surface.
Print streptavidin as lines for RGD gradients using microcontact printing.
Create adhesive patterns by printing matrix proteins using microcontact printing or dip-pen lithography.
Treat the patterned side of PDMS stamps in UV and ozone for 1.5 hours.
Alternatively, use a plasma cleaner to treat the PDMS stamp for a shorter time.
Place and spread 10 μl streptavidin (1 mg/ml in PBS) onto the treated PDMS stamp.
Leave the PDMS stamp with streptavidin for 1 hour in a humid chamber.
Remove excess streptavidin from the stamp using tissue paper.
Air dry the stamp for approximately 1 minute.
Lightly press the stamp onto the PLL-PEG-biotin-coated glass coverslip.
If fluorescent streptavidin was used, examine the pattern under an epifluorescence microscope.
Store printed surfaces in a desiccator.
Mix 1 part of 1 mg/ml streptavidin or streptavidin-AlexaFluor350 with 10 parts of glycerol (v/v).
Load 5 μl of the mixture onto the cantilever.
Begin the printing process as described in the operation manual of the dip pen lithography instrument.
Adjust printing speed, contact time of the cantilever on the surface or vertical distance of the cantilever to the surface to reduce the spot size to approximately 5 μm.
Print dots in a line with row and column separation set to 10-15 μm.
Store printed surfaces in a desiccator.
Adhere streptavidin-coated or -patterned glass coverslips onto the sticky side of the sticky-Slide Chemotaxis 3D device.
Seal the edges of the device with a thin layer of warmed Vaseline.
Apply a second layer of sealing using a mixture of 1 part Vaseline to 1 part paraffin wax (w/w).
Fill the channel of the device with 6 μl PBS.
Fill one reservoir with 70 μl of 0.03 μg/μl biotin-4-fluorescein in PBS.
Fill the other reservoir with 70 μl of 0.03 μg/μl biotin-RGD in PBS.
Incubate the samples at RT in the dark for 1 hr.
Remove the biotin solutions from the device.
Rinse the surface twice with PBS while still attached to the microfluidic device.
Mark the direction of the adhesive gradient.
Store the device filled with PBS at 4 °C if necessary, ensuring it does not dry out.
Analyze the adhesive gradient using a fluorescent microscope if required.
Wash cells three times with PBS.
Incubate cells with 1 μM Syto 64 Red in culture media for 45 min.
Wash cells three times with PBS after incubation.
Count fluorescently labelled cells.
Split counted cells into two tubes of equal cell numbers.
Wash and resuspend one tube of cells with media containing chemoattractant (low glucose DMEM with 10% FBS).
Wash and resuspend the other tube of cells in media without chemoattractant (DMEM with 0% FBS).
Ensure final concentration of cells in each tube is 5 x 10^5 cells/ml.
Remove all solutions from the microfluidic device.
Place the microfluidic device on the microscope stage.
Load 70 μl of cells (5 x 10^5 cells/ml in 0% FBS DMEM) into one reservoir.
Load 70 μl of HeLa cells (5 x 10^5 cells/ml in 10% FBS DMEM) into another reservoir.
Loosely place a tape over the reservoirs to avoid evaporation.
If cells on the surface are pre-incubated prior to imaging, load them into the device in growth media without the gradient.
Replace the media with gradient media: DMEM without FBS in one reservoir and DMEM with 10% FBS in the other.
Switch on the microscope (Nikon Ti-E) and warm up the stage at least 1 hour before starting the experiment.
Ensure that the channel of the microfluidic device is in the field of view and cells are in focus.
Select image acquisition parameters such as exposure times and fluorescent filters.
Capture a sequence of bright field and fluorescence images to track cells over time points (e.g., every 15 minutes for 16 hours).
Analyze data with appropriate software such as ImageJ Manual Tracking or Ibidi Chemotaxis and Migration Tool.
